I know some people are all about overclocking various computer components such as graphics cards to achieve a performance gain, but is that gain really worth the potential degradation to your hardware? I feel like everyone I have met who does it seems to do it because it makes them feel cool and like they pulled one over on the big corporations rather than because it makes sense to do on a regular basis.
Does the benefits of overclocking your computer hardware outweigh the risks?
Depends on what you're doing man. What do you plan on using your computer for?
Recreational gaming and the usual every day things. Occasionally some miscellaneous big number/data crunching. When is it worth it to do?

In my opinion it doesn't. System stability far outweighs any clock speed gains.

Besides, if you watch a 'Data Structures and Algorithms' course on YT you learn that these performance gains are only marginal. The real performance gains are determined by the algorithm. We are talking orders of magnitude here,

I don't see any point to it.

From a graphics card standpoint, In most cases you can get the (overclocked) performance out of a card that is only a fraction more then the one you are overclocking. So why not just buy the slightly better card?

And how fast those things get out of date, if you are really into gaming and "number crunching" you should really just set aside a few bucks a month and upgrade your card as need be.

It's like buying a 4 cylinder and then trying to get 6 cylinder performance out of it year after year, why not just buy a 6 and then run it normal.

And from what I've seen, you don't even get very much out of overclocking. Overclock the best graphics card of 2013 and you will end up with a $120 graphics card form 2015.

It depends on your hardware and, of course, on what are you doing with your PC. For example, if you have an unlocked i5 or i7, you can overclock it without any risk withing some limits. If you do video editing, simulations etc, you may want to squeeze every drop of performance. The lifetime of your CPU will decrease, but it's not an issue because you will change your hardware anyways, exception if you plan to keep your PC for 10-15 years.

PS: I talked about CPU overclocking. The only reason to overclock your memory is to get better scores in benchmark (or if your GPU is integrated in your CPU)... You can overclock your GPU though, GTX 970/980 get some nice results.

If we take out the possible equipment wear and instability out of the equation, you are left with elevated power consumption and with it a bigger electricity bill, so if you for example over clock everything 25% higher, your power usage and with that thermal output will rise atleast 25%. So if the added cost in electricity and heat pushed into the room the the machine is in is acceptable then it outweights the risks. Also, the more you overclock the more you run at the risk that something bad happens, conversely if you arent planning on overclocking one might want to buy the AMD E series or the intel T or S series that have almost as good stock performance but lower power consumption as they are optimized for low power and not overclockability the way they were binned when produced.
